notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 142, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Title and Setting

**"A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave. A Prayer."**

The Hebrew word *maskil* likely means "instruction" — a psalm teaching by example how to pray in distress. Matthew Henry (cited in Spurgeon) says David "learned on his knees, and so learned that he desired to teach others." The cave is probably Adullam (1 Samuel 22) or possibly En Gedi (1 Samuel 24). Psalm 57 shares the same cave-title. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/ ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

G. Campbell Morgan captures the two threads running through the psalm: "the terrible sense of helplessness and hopelessness so far as man is concerned" alongside "the determined application of the helpless soul to Jehovah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Gill notes the psalm also represents "the troubles of David, and of the Messiah his antitype, and is applicable to the church of God, or to any particular soul when in distress." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

---

## Verse 1

**"I cry aloud to the LORD; I lift my voice to the LORD for mercy."**

David's cry is more than an appeal for help — it is a declaration of allegiance to Yahweh. He refuses to cry to pagan gods. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Spurgeon notes the repetition ("with my voice … with my voice"): David "dwells upon the fact that he spoke aloud in prayer" and "it was evidently well impressed upon his memory." Caves, he adds, "make good closets for prayer; their gloom and solitude are helpful to the exercise of devotion." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Kidner compares David to Bartimaeus in the Gospels: he "knows the value of refusing to relapse into silence. That way lies despair." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Gill explains "crying" is explained by "making supplication" — "praying to the Lord in an humble manner for grace and mercy, and not pleading merit and worthiness." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

Steven Cole (bible.org) emphasises that the psalm "teaches us how to pray when we feel trapped and alone." Prayer should be "heartfelt and honest, but always in submission to God and His sovereign will." (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-142-trapped-alone)

---

## Verse 2

**"I pour out my complaint before Him; I reveal my trouble to Him."**

The Hebrew word rendered "complaint" is better translated "my troubled thoughts" or "my meditation" (Kidner, Barnes). It is not complaint *about* God but the honest pouring out of inner turmoil. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/ ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Spurgeon says: "If he poured it out before man he might only receive contempt … he resolved upon an outpouring before God alone, since he would pity and relieve." He adds that we show our trouble before the Lord "not that he may see it, but that we may see him. It is for our relief, not for his information." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Maclaren likewise says: "The outpouring of complaint is not meant to tell Jehovah what He does not know. It is for the complainer's relief." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Cole warns against anyone who would use this verse to justify "telling God off": that "encourages people to sin by railing at the loving, all-wise Sovereign of the universe." Honesty in prayer, yes — but always with a submissive heart. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-142-trapped-alone)

Neale and Littledale (cited in Spurgeon): "Those words teach us that in prayer we should not try to keep anything back from God, but should show him all that is in our hearts." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

---

## Verse 3

**"Although my spirit grows faint within me, You know my way. Along the path I travel they have hidden a snare for me."**

Ellicott renders the Hebrew literally: "in the muffling upon me of my spirit" — when David's spirit was "so wrapped in trouble and gloom … that I could not see the path before me." At that moment, "Thou (emphatic) knewest my path." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/142.htm)

Spurgeon: "David was a hero, and yet his spirit sank: he could smite a giant down, but he could not keep himself up. He did not know his own path, nor feel able to bear his own burden." His comfort was that God knew what David himself could not grasp. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Meyer (cited in Guzik): "Then it is an infinite solace to look up into the face of the Father, and say: Before I was born, or took the first steps on this path … Thou knewest it; and Thou must have known that it was not too hard." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Gill: the hidden snares refer to Saul's men lying in ambush. The clause "then Thou knewest my path" indicates that God sees and "approves of the way, of the life and conversation of his people in general; and particularly observes what way they take under affliction, which is to apply to him for help." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary adds: "I had not to tell thee because thou didst not know, but to relieve my own feelings." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-142.html)

---

## Verse 4

**"Look to my right and see; no one attends to me. There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul."**

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew is actually in the imperative — "Look to the right and see!" — which makes the psalm "livelier." The "right hand" is where a protector, advocate, or legal counsel would stand in Hebrew thought (cf. Psalm 16:8; 109:31; 110:5; 121:5). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/142.htm)

Maclaren: "The 'right hand' is the place for a champion or helper, but this lonely sufferer's is unguarded." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

VanGemeren: "The 'right' signifies the place where one's witness or legal council stood … He has no one to defend him against the adversaries." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Spurgeon poignantly says: "When a person is in ill odour it is wonderful how weak the memories of his former friends become: they quite forget, they refuse to know. … It is better to be opposed by foes than to be forsaken by friends." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Gill adds that David's looking "on my right hand, and beheld" (some read it as looking both right and left) yielded nothing: "no man that would know me … refuge failed me." Yet he qualifies: "that is, very few; otherwise there were some that were concerned for him, as the men that were with him, and Jonathan." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: David "looked about … for human aid, but there was no one who would so much as know me. I was utterly deserted in my trouble." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-142.html)

Matthew Henry sees David here as a type of Christ, "who, in his sufferings for us, was forsaken of all men, even of his own disciples, and trod the wine-press alone." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/142.htm — search excerpt)

Cole at bible.org stresses the practical application: "You don't have to be in his exact circumstances to have the same feelings" — whether from guilt, life-dominating sin, or the cost of Christian commitment. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-142-trapped-alone)

---

## Verse 5

**"I cry to You, O LORD: 'You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.'"**

This is the turning point. After looking around and finding no help from men, David looks up. Spurgeon calls it "a grand confession of faith": "Not thou hast provided me a refuge, but thou, thyself, art my refuge." He fled to God alone. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Spurgeon notes a "progressive repetition" through the psalm: "he cried first, but he said afterwards: his cry was bitter, but his saying was sweet." He adds: "If David had not cried he would not have said; and if the Lord had not been his refuge he would never have been his portion. The lower step is as needful as the higher." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Gill: "a refuge the Lord is to all his people in time of trouble … and such is Christ to all sensible sinners that flee unto him, Hebrews 6:18." As for "portion," it is "a large, immense, and inconceivable portion; he and all his perfections, purposes, promises, and blessings, being included in it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

Kidner: "To say 'my portion' goes as far beyond this as love goes beyond fear. [The Good News Bible] brings out the great force of this word by the phrase 'you are all I want'." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

David says this is his portion "in the land of the living" — not only in the age to come, but in the here and now. Spurgeon: "It is sometimes easier to believe in a portion in heaven than in a portion upon earth: we could die more easily than live, at least we think so. But there is no living in the land of the living like living upon the living God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

The Pulpit Commentary: "When men's fathers and mothers forsake them, the Lord taketh them up (Psalms 27:10)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-142.html)

---

## Verse 6

**"Listen to my cry, for I am brought quite low. Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me."**

David once again brings his cry honestly, "confessing his low circumstances." He did not pretend everything was fine. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Spurgeon notes the argument from weakness: "Gracious men may not only be low, but very low; and this should not be a reason for their doubting the efficacy of their prayers, but rather a plea with the Lord why they should have special attention." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

The admission "they are stronger than I" is striking. Guzik comments: "The one who killed Goliath felt himself to be very weak — and actually, that was a good place for David to be. God's strength would soon flood his life." Spurgeon's sermon (cited by Guzik) adds: "What was the way to Jerusalem for David? What was the way to the throne? Well, it was round by the cave of Adullam." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the historical situation: "In the cave of Adullam David had but four hundred outlaws to defend him against Saul, who was at the head of all the thousands of Israel." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-142.html)

Gill: Saul had "three thousand chosen men … veteran troops … David had about six hundred men, and these poor mean creatures, such as were in distress, in debt, and discontented." So too, "the spiritual enemies of the Lord's people are stronger than they." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

---

## Verse 7

**"Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name. The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me."**

"Prison" is almost certainly figurative. Kidner: "'My soul' is frequently a longer way of saying 'me'." VanGemeren adds: "'Prison' may denote actual imprisonment but may also be a metaphor for his desperate condition." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Spurgeon: "The cave was not half such a dungeon to David's body as persecution and temptation made for his soul. To be exiled from the godly is worse than imprisonment." His motive for deliverance is not personal comfort but praise: "That God may be glorified is another notable plea for a suppliant." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Matthew Henry applies it spiritually: "the souls of good men are often straitened by doubts and fears, cramped and fettered through the weakness of faith … and it is then their duty and interest to apply themselves to God, and beg of him to set them at liberty." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/142.htm — search excerpt)

The Hebrew verb for "shall surround me" can also mean "shall crown me." Trapp notes: "shall encircle me, as wondering at thy goodness in my deliverance; or they shall set the crown on mine head." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

Gill: "when delivered, they should flock to him and come about him, to see him and look at him, as a miracle of mercy, whose deliverance was marvellous; and to congratulate him upon it, and to join with him in praises." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

Spurgeon closes his exposition beautifully: "When we can begin a psalm with crying, we may hope to close it with singing. The voice of prayer soon awakens the voice of praise." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

Horne (cited in Guzik): "This prayer of David was heard and answered; he was delivered from his persecutors, enlarged from his distress, exalted to the throne, and joined by all the tribes of Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

The psalm's arc moves from complaint (v.2) to praise, from isolation (v.4) to companionship, from weakness (v.6) to confidence in God's bounty. Morgan: "In spite of all the opposition of men he realized that his God would deal bountifully with him, therefore instead of his foes, he would find himself surrounded by the righteous." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

---

## Differences Among Protestant Traditions

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** The Treasury of David treats the psalm as a model for the individual believer's prayer life — intensely personal and experiential. Spurgeon stresses the believer's direct access to God without human mediation ("he did not go round about to men, but he ran straight forward to Jehovah") and the psalm's movement from "crying" to "singing." The cave becomes a metaphor for the soul's trials where God alone suffices. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps142.php)

**Reformed / Evangelical (bible.org – Steven Cole):** Cole, writing from a conservative evangelical perspective, emphasises the sovereignty of God in ordaining trials. He insists that honest complaint to God must always be "in submission to God and His sovereign will," explicitly rejecting any notion of "telling God off." Prayer is not to inform God but "to prepare us to receive from Him the things we ask." Cole cites Jonathan Edwards: prayer is "not … to inform God … but rather suitably to affect our own hearts." (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-142-trapped-alone)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik):** Guzik draws on a wide range of commentators (Spurgeon, Maclaren, Kidner, Morgan, VanGemeren) and stresses the emotional and experiential dimensions — the "terrible sense of helplessness," the declaration of allegiance to Yahweh over pagan gods, and David's confidence that God would act in the "here and now" ("in the land of the living"). The emphasis falls on God's present deliverance and David's journey from weakness to strength through prayer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-142/)

**Charismatic / Reformed Charismatic (Sam Storms):** The search excerpt from Storms' article (title: "No One Cares for my Soul") indicates he reads the psalm as speaking to seasons of abandonment and isolation, with David longing for deliverance "because it will afford … the opportunity to again praise God for his bountiful provision." The righteous will surround him "for you will deal bountifully with me." (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/no-one-cares-for-my-soul--psalm-142- — search excerpt)

*Note: I was unable to retrieve full articles from specifically Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or specifically Reformed (ligonier.org, monergism.com) sites within the available search and fetch limits. The Matthew Henry commentary (used across traditions) and Gill (Baptist) do provide substantial traditional Protestant readings.*

---

## Other Views

**Catholic (Augustine):** The search located Augustine's *Exposition on Psalm 142* at New Advent. Augustine reads the psalm Christologically — the title "when he was in the cave" points to Christ in the cave of the tomb, or Christ in His humility. The "cave" represents Christ's incarnation: He hid His divinity in the "cave" of human flesh. The "prison" of verse 7 Augustine interprets as the prison of mortality and sin from which Christ liberates the soul. I was unable to fetch the full text, but the URL is available: (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801142.htm)

**Gill on Messianic Application:** Gill (18th-century Baptist) also reads the psalm as representing "the troubles of David, and of the Messiah his antitype," noting its application to "the church of God, or to any particular soul when in distress." He applies "bring my soul out of prison" Christologically, while firmly rejecting the Roman Catholic reading of "prison" as purgatory: "Not out of purgatory, to which some Popish writers wrest these words very absurdly." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/142.htm)

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes):** I was unable to fetch the NET Bible notes within the limit. The search did locate a reference to bible.org's NET-based tagging but not a full set of translation notes for Psalm 142. (A search for "Psalm 142 netbible.org notes" was among those cut off by the search limit.)

**Modern Scholarship (bibleodyssey.org):** I was unable to search this site within the available limits. No results were obtained.

---

## Summary of What I Could Not Find

Despite the constraints, the materials retrieved represent a broad spectrum: a classic Baptist exposition (Spurgeon), an 18th-century Baptist scholarly commentary (Gill), a conservative evangelical/pastoral treatment (bible.org/Cole), a charismatic/Pentecostal verse-by-verse (Guzik/Enduring Word), Anglican-informed older scholarship (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary), and Reformed-leaning older works (Matthew Henry). The Catholic/Patristic reading by Augustine was located but not fetched. Specifically Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, and Eastern Orthodox sources could not be reached within the tool limits. Prosperity/Word of Faith readings of this psalm did not appear in any search results.
